title: IAG offers to dump WA NRMA brand
full_text:
Insurance Australia Group has pledged to offload its NRMA-branded home and car insurance business in Western Australia in an attempt to convince the competition regulator to approve its acquisition of the insurance operations of Royal Automobile Club in the state.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission opposed the $1.4 billion deal in the initial phase of its review, but is now considering whether it has public benefits following a series of commitments made by IAG.
IAG's latest concessions involve the sale of renewal rights for NRMA's existing customers to another insurer, which could reduce the combined market share of the merged companies to below 50 per cent.
The ACCC's concerns centred on the deal giving the combined group a market share of between 55 per cent and 65 per cent in motor vehicle insurance in Western Australia, and between 50 per cent and 60 per cent for home and contents insurance.
The NRMA book made up about 14 per cent of the combined business, according to JPMorgan analyst Siddharth Parameswaran.
Suncorp, Allianz and QBE, along with mid-tier insurers Auto & General, Youi and Hollard, operate in the state and could be potential buyers of the renewal rights. RAC could seek to pick up the offloaded customers in future by competing in the market.
"In our view, the renewal rights sale concession increases the prospects of a deal proceeding," said UBS analyst Kieren Chidgey.
In another concession, IAG said it would offer RAC home insurance products in the north of the state, including Karratha, Port Hedland and Broome, providing cyclone protection by tapping IAG's reinsurance program. In another sweetener, IAG, which did a similar deal to buy RAC's insurance operations in Queensland, a deal that was approved by the ACCC, also said it would invest $20 million to support "community resilience-building initiatives" in the state over the next decade.
Appearing at The Australian Financial Review Energy and Climate Summit, Julie Batch, who runs IAG's Australian retail insurance operations, pledged to roll out road safety programs and initiatives to support the transition to electric vehicles, including specialised EV repair services. The ACCC also expressed concerns about the effect of the deal on smash repairers.
IAG said the public benefits commitments did not alter the transaction's underlying strategic or financial rationale. At the time it was announced in May 2025, IAG said it would add $1.5 billion in gross written premium and provide geographic diversification. By taking on more risk in northern Western Australia and selling its NRMA book, the potential earnings per share upside would be reduced, said Parameswaran.
IAG shares fell 1.8 per cent to $8.27 on Wednesday, in line with declines for rivals Suncorp and QBE.
The ACCC initially expressed concerns about the deal in September last year, and knocked it back again under the new merger regime last month.
"We are proposing additional commitments and accountabilities in relation to product pricing and competitiveness of the RAC insurance offering," said IAG chief executive Nick Hawkins.
ANZ was able to use public benefit arguments to convince the Australian Competition Tribunal to overturn the ACCC's decision to block its acquisition of Suncorp under the previous rules.
